document_title: The Sentence That Isn't in Executive Order 14421
post_copy:
One sentence in federal law says the grid reliability rules don't apply to Alaska. Executive Order 14421 carries no sentence like it.

The order borrows the statute's definition of the bulk-power system almost word for word. It adds a threshold the statute never had at 69,000 volts. The Alaska Energy Authority puts the Alaska Intertie at 138 kilovolts and calls it part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System. The Railbelt Reliability Council calls the same grid islanded.

DOE takes written comments through October 9th, 2026. Its rules are due 120 days from the order.

Both definitions sit side by side in the deck at identical size, and the order's stated reason names data centers and artificial intelligence.

Which Alaska institution should put the Railbelt's voltages in front of DOE before that window closes?

#AlaskaEnergy #Railbelt #BulkPowerSystem

editor_notes_for_email:
Read slide 04, slide 08 and slide 07 before posting.

Slide 04 is the deck's whole argument and the frame most likely to be misread. It sets the statute's definition and the order's definition at identical size, measure and colour, and the only difference drawn is a gold line under the right column. The missing Alaska sentence in Executive Order 14421 is drawn as an absence of ink, never as a deletion, because C12 is an absence claim at 0.85 confidence. Nothing on that frame says Alaska is excluded or included, and nothing should be added in a comment that does.

Slide 08 is the counterweight and it is what keeps this deck from reading as an accusation. The Alaska Energy Authority calls the Alaska Intertie an integral part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System (C31), which cuts toward the order reaching Alaska, and it is given the same page size and the same highlighter length as the Railbelt Reliability Council's word islanded (C24). If a reader takes the deck as a claim that Alaska is out, that slide is the answer, and the equality is measurable rather than asserted.

Slide 07 carries every number someone will screenshot. The DeepGreen row is phantom-dashed and labelled PROPOSED because Project No. 15423-000 is a preliminary permit and not a built line (C37, C38). The ladder is linear in kilovolts against a printed scale, so the distance between 138 kV and the order's 69 kV is measured rather than claimed. One string on that slide compresses two sources. The foot reads that five utilities run nearly 700 miles between those towns, where the council's own wording is five load-serving utilities interconnected across nearly 700 miles (C26, C28) and the four towns come from its footprint description (C25). If a Railbelt engineer pushes on that sentence, quote the council's wording back.

FOUR THINGS THE BUILD CHANGED against the storyboard, all of them in copy that actually rendered, so the strings here are the render and not the dossier. Slide 05's body was rewritten, the four quoted categories now live in the four struck rows and the body attributes the supporting critical infrastructure qualifier to the order rather than stating it flat. Slide 07's ladder rows were retitled and its strip caption folded into the foot, so a separate five utilities line no longer exists as its own string. Slide 08's foot now says the council SAYS it serves nearly three-quarters of Alaskans, which attributes C27 on the slide as the hedge list requires. Slide 09 dropped the 180 day Federal Acquisition Regulation line, so C11 is verified in claims.json and prints nowhere in the deck, and the tag now carries only the 120 day rule deadline.

Nothing in the locked caption reads as a factual error against claims.json. The 120 day line matches C10, the October 9th, 2026 date matches C16, and both Alaska Energy Authority phrases match C30 and C31 word for word.

slides.beat: Cover. The claim struck into a transformer's rating plate.
strings: One sentence of federal law names Alaska. The order doesn't.
BULK POWER SYSTEM . 69 KV AND ABOVE

slides.beat: The sentence itself, on the page it lives on.
strings: "The provisions of this section do not apply to Alaska or Hawaii."
That is the entire subsection. It sits in the electric reliability section of the Federal Power Act, the section that created the national reliability organization regime.
16 U.S.C. 824o(k) SUBSECTION HEADED ALASKA AND HAWAII

slides.beat: The order's own stated reason, in its own words.
strings: "The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system."

slides.beat: The hinge. Both definitions in one frame, word for word the same, then diverging.
strings: Two definitions, word for word the same.
"facilities and control systems necessary for operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network"
The statute carries a subsection about Alaska. The order carries a sentence about 69,000 volts.

slides.beat: The inventory. The covered equipment, struck down the tank as a field table.
strings: What the order calls covered equipment.
Section 5(b) lists these among the bulk-power system electric equipment the order reaches. The last of them is qualified in the order as supporting critical infrastructure.

slides.beat: Breather. One line in the country, at twice the threshold.
strings: The Alaska Intertie runs 170 miles between Willow and Healy. The Alaska Energy Authority puts it at 138 kilovolts. The order's line is 69,000 volts.

slides.beat: Keepable data. The voltage ladder and the Railbelt strip, measured against the gold datum.
strings: Three Alaska figures sit above the line and none below it. Five utilities run nearly 700 miles between those towns.

slides.beat: Counterweight. Alaska's own agencies use both words, islanded and interconnected.
strings: Alaska's own agencies use both words.

The Railbelt Reliability Council calls the Railbelt grid islanded. The Alaska Energy Authority calls the Alaska Intertie an integral part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System. Both statements are on the record and they point in opposite directions.
RRC SAYS IT SERVES NEARLY THREE-QUARTERS OF ALASKANS

slides.beat: The window. Question A-2, the four words absent from it, and the date.
strings: Question A-2 of the DOE request for information asks commenters to identify any equipment-specific voltage, capacity, connectivity, function, location, or criticality thresholds. The words Alaska, Hawaii, islanded and non-contiguous appear nowhere in it.

slides.beat: Close. The honest position, and one ask.
strings: Nobody has said Alaska is in. Nobody has said Alaska is out.
Which threshold should Alaska ask DOE to write down?
